#4345. Arc Raiders has proven that extraction shooters can be popular, with over 4 million copies sold in under two weeks

Arc Raiders has sold even more copies, which we should've guessed, given that the game keeps breaking its own concurrent player records.

It’s pretty clear at this stage that Arc Raiders is one of the biggest launches of 2025. More interesting than the numbers themselves, however, is that this is an extraction shooter - a subgenre which has typically been thought of as niche.

If you’ve been paying the PvPvE game any attention, you could easily see how (and why) it keeps breaking its own records.

Today, publisher Nexon announced in a press release (via Gematsu) that Arc Raiders has now sold over 4 million copies. The game came out on October 30, which means it managed to sell that many copies in a little over 10 days.

The news comes on the same day that developer Embark Studios announced that the game had more than 700,000 concurrent players across all platforms over the weekend. Over the same weekend on Steam alone, Arc Raiders broke its own Steam concurrent record with a new peak of 462,488 players - which is a significant chunk of that 700,000+ player base.

This marks the second time the extraction shooter has broken its own concurrent player records, which is something very few games have managed in the past. Arc Raiders remains a top-seller, too. On Steam, it’s currently the second-best seller globally (by revenue), sitting just below Counter-Strike 2.

“The many different ways you play and participate in ARC Raiders have completely blown us away, going far beyond what we ever imagined. You surprise us, you outsmart us, and you keep us on our toes. We wouldn’t have it any other way,” the developer wrote on Twitter.

Embark recently published a roadmap to highlight all the new content coming to the game over the remainder of this year. The first new map is set to arrive this month alongside new Arc units, new gameplay items, new events and more.

Just over the weekend, the game received several new Map Conditions that completely alter the way they play. The developer has already rolled out a couple of updates since launch, in order to tackle exploits and fix a few launchday bugs.

If you’re currently hooked on this gem of a game, we guarantee that our Arc Raiders gameplay tips will have at least one you didn’t know about. We also have more guides on how to find some of the more elusive items in the game, such as olives, lemons and apricots, and prickly pears.

#4343. Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke

New preliminary research involving more than 440,000 American adults has uncovered a concerning association between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease, particularly stroke. The findings suggest that even occasional marijuana use may be linked to higher odds of cardiovascular problems, raising new questions about the health effects of a substance that is becoming increasingly common across the United States.

The research, presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, found that the association was not limited to people who frequently used cannabis. It also appeared across different methods of consumption (smoked or edible, etc.). Researchers emphasized that cannabis use should be considered when discussing heart health and stroke prevention.

Scientific Sessions 2026 took place November 6 through 9 in Chicago, bringing together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, clinical advances, and emerging evidence.

Cannabis refers to the plant itself, while marijuana is a commonly used term for cannabis products containing enough THC to produce psychoactive effects.

Marijuana Use Is Rising Across the United States

"Previous research has indicated that cannabis use is rapidly increasing in the United States, with 1 in 6 adults in 2024 reporting having used it within the last month, up from 1 in 10 in 2020 -- a 51% increase," said study author Aabha Divya, M.B.B.S., M.Ch., an assistant professor in the division of cardiothoracic surgery at the Tulane University School of Medicine in New Orleans.

Earlier research conducted between 2016 and 2020 had already identified associations between cannabis consumption and unfavorable cardiovascular outcomes. Those findings also suggested that using cannabis more frequently during a given month was connected to greater cardiovascular risk.

However, the evidence has not always been consistent. With recreational marijuana becoming legal in more places and cannabis products increasingly available, Divya and colleagues wanted to investigate these possible health effects in a larger population.

"We wanted to expand on this earlier work because cannabis use has become increasingly common in the United States, as recreational legalization and commercial availability of various products with cannabis have also expanded. Previous studies have raised concerns about possible cardiovascular effects; however, the results have not been consistent," Divya said.

The researchers examined information collected through the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), a large telephone survey of American adults. They combined responses from jurisdictions that collected information about cannabis consumption between 2020 and 2024.

Participants answered questions about their marijuana use and whether a healthcare professional had ever diagnosed them with cardiovascular conditions, including a heart attack, stroke, or coronary heart disease.

Even Occasional Marijuana Use Was Linked to Higher Stroke Odds

One of the most striking findings was that infrequent cannabis use was associated with cardiovascular problems. In fact, the researchers did not find the steady increase in cardiovascular risk with more frequent use that they had expected.

The analysis revealed several important associations:

These findings were unexpected because the relationship between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease did not consistently become stronger as consumption increased.

"We were surprised to find that the link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease was not straightforward. We expected that the chances of heart disease would gradually rise as people used cannabis more often, but that wasn't the case. Both low-use and heavy-use groups had higher odds of developing heart disease," Divya said.

Although the study cannot establish that marijuana directly causes strokes or other cardiovascular conditions, the findings suggest that occasional consumption should not automatically be considered free of potential cardiovascular concerns.

"As cannabis use becomes more common, it is increasingly important that people and their healthcare professionals include it in conversations about cardiovascular health, just as they discuss tobacco, alcohol and other commonly used substances," she added.

Experts Urge Greater Attention to Cannabis and Heart Health

Robert L. Page II, Pharm.D., M.S.P.H., FAHA, who led the writing group responsible for the American Heart Association's 2020 cannabis scientific statement, said the findings add to growing concerns about marijuana's possible cardiovascular effects.

One challenge in evaluating those effects is that many cannabis users also smoke tobacco. Because tobacco is already an established cardiovascular risk factor, separating its effects from those of cannabis can be difficult.

Page, who was not involved in the research, explained why the new findings deserve attention.

"Unfortunately, many patients who use cannabis may also smoke tobacco, which completely clouds the issue when addressing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk. In patients who use both, cannabis has always been considered an innocent bystander; however, this is not the case. This is the second observational study to suggest that cannabis exposure (without tobacco smoking) may be a potential risk factor for developing cardiovascular disease. Overall, cannabis is beginning to emerge as a major contributor to premature heart disease in young and older adults, which can lead to serious cardiovascular events. To this end, clinicians should be addressing cannabis use with their patients as they would tobacco use when considering the risk of cardiovascular disease."

Page is a professor in the department of clinical pharmacy and the department of physical medicine/rehabilitation at the University of Colorado Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences in Aurora, Colorado.

How Researchers Studied Nearly Half a Million Americans

The analysis included 442,906 adults living in the United States (average age of 49 years; approximately half women). Their responses came from telephone surveys conducted through the BRFSS.

Researchers used survey information collected from 2020 through 2024, focusing on states that had included an optional marijuana questionnaire. Between 16 and 24 states participated in this portion of the survey each year, meaning the analysis did not represent every state.

Participants reported how many days they had consumed cannabis during the preceding month. The questions covered multiple ways of using marijuana (smoking, vaping or ingesting gummies or other cannabis-containing foods).

The researchers divided participants into four categories based on their reported use:

Participants also indicated whether they had ever received a diagnosis of heart attack, heart disease, heart-related chest pain, or stroke.

To better distinguish the association with cannabis from other potential explanations, the researchers accounted for numerous established cardiovascular risk factors. These included demographic characteristics, tobacco smoking, alcohol consumption, obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, physical inactivity, education, and income.

Why the Findings Do Not Prove Marijuana Causes Strokes

Despite the large number of participants, the study has several limitations that affect how its findings should be interpreted.

First, the analysis examined associations between reported cannabis use and previously diagnosed cardiovascular conditions at a single point in time. This means researchers could not determine whether marijuana use preceded the cardiovascular problems or whether it directly contributed to them.

The information also depended on participants accurately recalling and reporting their cannabis consumption and medical histories (making them subject to potential errors in memory). Such reports may not always reflect actual patterns of use or diagnoses.

Another limitation was the lack of information about the strength of the cannabis products participants consumed or the quantities they used. Without those details, the researchers could not evaluate whether THC potency or the amount consumed influenced the observed associations.

The researchers also acknowledged that some participants may have reduced or discontinued cannabis consumption after being diagnosed with cardiovascular disease. As a result, the group reporting no cannabis use in the previous month may have included former users.

These uncertainties make it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how consumption frequency affects cardiovascular health. Nevertheless, the findings add to growing evidence that cannabis use deserves closer examination as a possible factor in heart disease and stroke.

As marijuana becomes more widely available and its use continues to increase, researchers and healthcare professionals are emphasizing the importance of discussing cannabis alongside other substances that may affect cardiovascular health.

#4342. Arc Raiders' new map will be unlocked through a community event that starts today, and everyone has to donate

It looks like it's going to take the Arc Raiders community a bit of work to unlock the game's next map.

As many of Arc Raiders’ regular players predicted, the game’s first post-launch map won’t just be available for everyone, it will instead be closely tied to a community event. Breaking New Ground is the name of that event, and it’s one where everyone will need to contribute in order to rebuild some old tunnels and unlock the way to Stella Montis.

The event kicks off today alongside the release of the game’s latest patch. The ask is relatively simple: players must commit Basic Materials to the project so that the tunnels can be rebuilt. This option will be available to anyone who’s played at least five rounds.

If you’ve spent any time in Arc Raiders, you’ll know that Basic Materials are things like Metal parts, Fabric, Chemicals, Rubber Parts, and Plastic Parts - most of which are easy to find in the game’s various maps.

Even beyond the ultimate goal of unlocking the new map, donations will also reward you with Merits, which is a new event currency, though there’s a cap on how many you can earn.

Once enough materials have been collected, the next phase of the event, Staking Our Claim, will begin, which will bring a new progression track to the game, and make Stella Montis available for players to visit.

Developer Embark describes the new environment as unlike any that we have seen in the game so far. It’s a facility carved into the northern mountains, which means it’s going to have a near-pristine look; quite the contrast with the rest of the game’s environments.

Stella Montis also has its own Arc enemies, loot, schematics, and other gameplay items. You can look forward to coming across the Shredder, a close-quarter Arc unit exclusive to the new map for now.

Then there’s The Matriarch, a somehow even larger version of the Queen. Thankfully, it will only be available under a specific map condition, so you’re in no danger of running into her randomly. The update will also introduce a new legendary weapon, two new grenades, and three new mines.

Staking Our Claim will only run until December, which is when the next stage of the game’s roadmap will kick off. Then, the Cold Snap update will introduce the Flickering Flames event, the first snowfall Map Condition, and the Expedition Project voluntary wipe.

In case you’re still missing them, here’s how to find lemons and apricots, prickly pear, and olives.

Zenless Zone Zero’s latest Special Program was a big one, bringing us all the news about Version 2.4, the next major update. It’s called On the Precipice of the Abyss, and it will be available to download on November 26.

On the Precipice of the Abyss has tendrils in many areas of the game, touching several parts of its fiction as well as gameplay, so it’s one to watch out for.

Banyue is another S-Rank, though he’s a Fire Rupture Agent. He uses his martial arts expertise to create combinations of might and grandeur. Birkblick is Krampus' own proprietary lil bunny fella, who brings a sensor array that can transform into a cannon in combat, essentially tracking and immediately nuking targets. Then there’s Bild N. Boolok, a Support Agent-affiliated Physical damage dealing Bangboo bringing a giant block hammer to the fight to, well, smash enemies with.

It’s a bit of a winter party in Version 2.4, it seems, as the update will bring back Hugo (Attack - Ice), and Ellen (Attack - Ice), too.

You can also look forward to the return of the Bangboo auto chess event, which now includes PvE stages with unique rewards. In fact, playing this event is how you could get Bild N. Boolok for free. Lightstream Notes is another event that will be available for the duration of this update, and it will let you tag along with Ye Shunguang to New Eridu.

#4340. Rimac Is Reportedly Ending Nevera Production After Selling Just 71 Cars

The electric hypercar set plenty of records, but it may have come in well under the purportedly planned production run of 190 examples.

Rimac is ending production of its all-electric Nevera hypercar at the end of 2026, Germany’s Auto Motor und Sport reports. And somewhat surprisingly, the same report suggests that just 71 of 190 planned Reveras were built over the course of its production run.

The base Nevera, and its later Nevera R variant, have held a number of records, including the title of world’s quickest car, what was once the EV lap record at the Nürburgring Nordschleife, and a quarter-mile run under 7.9 seconds. Those numbers may not have been enough to make the model a hit with buyers, though. According to the report, 51 of a planned 150 base-model Neveras were built, and 20 out of a planned 40 Nevera Rs reached production.

While the apparent final tally of Nevera production is striking, it is part of a larger pattern of electric hypercars failing to find an audience. The Lotus Evija once competed directly with Rimac’s Nevera, but Lotus has since moved on to a hybrid supercar with V-8 power. Former Rimac stakeholder Porsche once considered its own electric hypercar, only to pivot to an internal-combustion supercar instead. Even as cars like the Tesla Roadster and Yangwang U9 Xtreme make headlines with record-setting stunts, there are questions on whether or not a conventional hypercar buyer would be interested in paying for an EV.

See all results for Rimac Nevera for sale near 80219

Whether or not the Nevera itself was a success, the halo car did succeed in raising Rimac’s profile. Namesake founder Mate Rimac is now fully in charge of Bugatti, and Rimac Technology provides electric powertrain components to major cars like the Porsche 911 Turbo S. As the most significant electric hypercar to reach the market to date—well, perhaps along with the closely related Pininfarina Battista—the few Neveras in private hands represent a major leap forward for both electric performance and the Rimac brand itself.

Fred Smith's love of cars comes from his fascination with auto racing. Unfortunately, that passion led him to daily drive a high-mileage, first-year Porsche Panamera. He is still thinking about the last lap of the 2011 Indianapolis 500.

#4339. Battlefield 6 gets a new map today alongside major changes to controller aim assist, and even more weapon dispersion tweaks

Right on schedule, the latest Battlefield 6 patch has arrived to kick off the next stage of Season 1.

Battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase. The game received a major update earlier today, version 1.1.2.0, which delivers a host of changes to the game, many of which have been expected.

The update, of course, also adds new content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.

We’ve known about the new content side of today’s patch for quite some time. The update kicks off the California Resistance stage of Season 1, which is the second of three. The new Eastwood map takes place in California, and it’s a map cut from the larger Battlefield Redsec battle royale map of Fort Lyndon.

There’s a new limited-time mode called Sabotage - a tactical, 8v8 mode where two teams attempt to destroy as many bomb sites as possible. The other big new feature that arrives today is Battle Pickups.

These are powerful weapons which can be found in specific game modes (and in Portal), scattered around the map for players to pick up and use. They have limited ammo that cannot be replenished, and deliver incredible firepower.

Redsec players have a new Gauntlet mission to look forward to that joins the existing modes. It’s called Rodeo and it involves a lot of vehicular action. Finally, everyone gets to unlock two new weapons: the the DB-12 shotgun, and the M327 Trait revolver sidearm. There’s also a new angled grip attachment.

The fixes and tweaks side of the patch is arguably the more interesting. Controller aim assist has received a big overhaul that essentially resets everything to open beta settings. The goal is to make infantry targeting more consistent.

Controller players actually get the bulk of the changes in this update, which also improves input latency and stick response. Several issues that reset aim assist values, or make it behave erratically, have been addressed.

The conversation around weapon bloom/spread doesn’t look like it’s ever going to end, because Battlefield Studios is yet again tuning gunplay to fix unintended dispersion behaviour, and decrease its intensity across the board.

Certain Challenges have had their description rewritten so their requirements can be better understood. Beyond that, you can expect several deployables to behave much more consistently, including several bug fixes there, too.

Head to the official blog for the full rundown of patch 1.1.2.0.

#4338. Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

Energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising new concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies. Products containing caffeine and other stimulants appeared far more frequently in reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks, and other heart problems than products without these ingredients.

The findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. People ages 18 to 34 accounted for a substantial share of the reported heart problems involving caffeinated products, according to independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.

Researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies. However, the unusually high frequency of certain cardiovascular events in FDA safety reports suggests that these widely available products deserve closer examination.

Growing Concerns About Energy Drinks and Heart Health

The energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade and exceeding $20 billion in 2024. Despite their popularity, scientists still have limited information about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and supplements containing stimulants.

Existing evidence suggests that consuming large amounts of caffeine can harm the cardiovascular system. Medical professionals have also documented cases of arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms) and sudden cardiac death following the consumption of these products. Some of these incidents involved young adults who had no previously identified risk factors for heart disease.

A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease indicates that most adults can generally consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily without significant safety concerns (the equivalent of up to 5, 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee).

However, caffeine concentrations can differ dramatically between products. Certain energy drinks provide up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee, while some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times the concentration found in coffee.

Another concern involves how these products are regulated. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies energy drinks and stimulant supplements as foods or dietary supplements rather than medications. As a result, they are not subject to the same safety testing requirements that medications must meet before entering the market.

"These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk," said study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, Virginia. "For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it's important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products."

FDA Reports Reveal Striking Differences in Cardiac Events

To investigate possible cardiovascular safety concerns, researchers examined a federal database containing reports of suspected adverse reactions to foods and dietary supplements. They compared products containing caffeine and other stimulants with products that did not contain these ingredients.

The comparison group included commonly consumed products such as soft drinks, smoothies, vitamins, protein bars, and meal replacement shakes. Researchers examined reports involving people ages 13 and older submitted between 2017 and 2025.

Several differences stood out in the analysis:

These differences describe how frequently certain medical problems appeared within the FDA reports. They do not mean that people consuming energy drinks face an 11 times greater actual risk of cardiac arrest or a 4.5 times greater risk of having a heart attack.

"Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain, or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products," Samayamanthula said.

Why Young Adults May Be Particularly Vulnerable

One of the most notable findings was the large proportion of cardiovascular reports involving younger adults. Researchers have not yet determined why the connection between stimulant products and reported heart problems appeared so frequently in this age group.

Several explanations are possible. Younger consumers may use energy drinks and stimulant supplements more often, increasing the likelihood that these products appear in reports of medical emergencies.

How the products are consumed could also influence the pattern. Potential contributing factors include the circumstances surrounding their use (for example, consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs). Some individuals may also have previously undiagnosed heart conditions that could make them more susceptible to cardiovascular complications.

These possibilities remain uncertain, and additional research will be needed to determine which factors, if any, help explain the unusually high reporting frequency among younger adults.

Do Energy Drinks Actually Cause Heart Attacks?

Although the results raise important questions about products containing concentrated caffeine and other stimulants, experts caution against interpreting the findings as proof of a direct cause.

"This study raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system," said Gregory M. Marcus, M.D., M.A.S., FAHA, chair of the 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease. "Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis. More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events."

Marcus did not participate in the research. He is a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine and serves as associate chief of the Cardiology for Research program at the University of California, San Francisco Health.

Because the analysis relied on reports submitted voluntarily to the FDA, it cannot establish whether the products themselves were responsible for the cardiovascular events. Other health conditions, behaviors, or circumstances may have played a role.

How Researchers Analyzed the FDA Safety Reports

The research team reviewed 28,345 reports of possible adverse events submitted to an FDA safety database from 2017 through 2025.

Of these, 854 reports involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. The remaining 27,491 reports concerned products without caffeine or stimulant ingredients and served as the comparison group.

Researchers classified products according to the ingredients they contained. The stimulant category included caffeine, methylxanthines (theobromine, guarana, yerba mate, green tea/coffee extracts) and sympathomimetics (synephrine, yohimbine, ephedra, DMAA, higenamine).

Rather than evaluating individual brands, the researchers grouped products by their ingredients. Consequently, the findings apply to broad categories of caffeinated and stimulant products and do not identify any particular brand as more dangerous than another.

The researchers also highlighted important limitations in the available data. Reports were voluntarily submitted by members of the public, consumers, healthcare professionals, and manufacturers, meaning that the database does not provide a complete record of everyone who experienced a possible adverse reaction.

Just as importantly, the researchers could not determine how many people consumed these products without developing cardiovascular problems. They also could not establish how many people experienced heart problems but never submitted a report.

Without those figures, the analysis cannot calculate the actual likelihood of a heart attack, cardiac arrest, or another cardiovascular event among consumers of energy drinks and stimulant supplements.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important safety signal. Researchers say more systematic monitoring and further studies are needed to determine whether these products contribute directly to serious heart problems, particularly among younger adults who frequently consume them.

#4335. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with... a questionable selection of maps, but at least the modes are good

If Redsec got you hooked on Battlefield gameplay but you never experienced traditional multiplayer in Battlefield 6, there's an upcoming moment you might want to pay attention to.

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has announced that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently launched Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

Instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two new maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

As for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two new maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

The miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 launched with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for new players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.

#4334. Major World War 2 Flight Sim Goes Free for a Limited Time

News Editor at DualShockers, 10+ years writing experience, OpenCritic-listed reviewer, Master’s Degree in Developmental Psychology

The Il-2 Sturmovik name has become associated with excellence in flight sims since its initial release on November 18, 2001.

Although the team behind the first launch is no longer around, the torchbearers at For-Games are marking the occasion by letting new players try out the cornerstone game of the second generation of the Il-2 Sturmovik series.

Korea: Il-2 Series is a promising start for the next generation of flight simulators.

Starting today, Il-2 Sturmovik: Battle of Stalingrad will be free to play on Steam, as part of the 25th anniversary celebration of the franchise. The flight simulator is also offering an 85% discount until November 15.

Il-2 Sturmovik: Battle of Stalingrad centers on the battle of the same name that raged from July 1942 until February 1943. Although the Germans, led by the 6th Army, managed to enter the city, a massive Soviet counterattack led by Marshall Georgy Zhukov in November trapped Axis forces in.

Codenamed Operation Uranus, this move kicked off a brutal siege that would lead to the annihilation of the 6th Army and the capture of its commander, Field Marshal Fiedrich Paulus. The German defeat marked the end of its expansionism to the East, and is often cited as the turning point of the war in Soviet favor.

The fight on the ground has become the stuff of legends, but airpower played a major part in the battle of Stalingrad.

A massive German bombardment turned the city to rubble in August 1942, killing thousands of civilians and destroying almost all houses in the city. The German Luftflotte 4 averaged 1000 sorties per day between August 23 and November 22, 1942, putting immense pressure on the strained Soviet defenders.

When Zhukov's counterattack closed the door on the German troops in the city, the Luftwaffe pivoted from offensive missions to airlift, using transports and bombers to haul supplies and wounded. German fighters and attack aircraft managed to inflict heavy losses on Soviet units during this period, but were comprehensively beaten on a strategic level.

The fight on the ground has become the stuff of legends, but airpower played a major part in the battle of Stalingrad.

Soviet aviation in Stalingrad was outmatched in both quality and numbers when the Axis offensive hit in the summer of 1942. Reinforcements in August eventually helped tip the scale in the Red Army's favor, especially with the widespread deployment of La-5 fighters, plus Il-2 and Pe-2 attack aircraft.

The siege of Stalingrad allowed Soviet fighters to hunt down German transports trying to reinforce the 6th Army, in turn forcing German fighters to dedicate more and more time protecting these. Eventually, Soviet fighter activity pushed the Germans to primarily fly transports at night, which became increasingly prohibitive once the winter set in.

Meanwhile, Il-2 Sturmovik attack aircraft used the increasingly thin German fighter cover to pound enemy frontlines. Il-2 and Pe-2 units also took the fight to German airfields, hammering aircraft on the ground and helping seal the fate of the trapped garrison.

On its own merits, Il-2 Sturmovik: Battle of Stalingrad is one of the most realistic and advanced flight simulators in the market, and it remains the leading World War 2 game in its category.

Players are able to fly eight different aircraft in the standard edition.

On top of that, the Il-2 Sturmovik structure allows owners of any edition to play across maps in multiplayer servers, which means you’ll get to experience some of the newer maps if you choose to fly online.

#4333. Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

The type of exercise you do may be more important for your bones than how long you spend doing it. Researchers at Semmelweis University have found that intense physical activity involving sudden bursts of movement, quick changes in direction, and sharp turns appears especially effective at stimulating new bone formation.

The findings, published in Sports Medicine - Open, suggest that certain fast-paced sports may provide greater benefits for bone metabolism than walking or conventional strength training. The research could help scientists develop more effective exercise recommendations for preserving bone health and reducing the risk of osteoporosis.

Why Exercise Intensity Matters for Bone Health

To investigate how different forms of exercise affect bones, the Semmelweis University team reviewed 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults.

Instead of relying on bone mineral density measurements, which can take considerable time to reveal changes, the researchers examined blood markers associated with the production of new bone tissue. These biological indicators can reveal how bones respond to exercise within a matter of weeks, allowing scientists to detect changes much sooner.

"What makes our study unique is that we examined not only the type of exercise - whether endurance, resistance, or combined training - but also exercise intensity, frequency, and duration. Our goal was to determine which forms of exercise stimulate bone metabolism most effectively and which appear to be less beneficial from this perspective," said Dr. Péter Ferdinandy, Vice-Rector for Science and Innovations at Semmelweis University and senior author of the study.

Football and Handball Show Surprising Bone Benefits

The strongest responses were associated with vigorous sports that repeatedly require players to accelerate, change direction, turn, and make powerful movements.

Recreational football and handball stood out in particular. These activities were linked to increases of up to 45-46 percent in blood markers associated with bone formation, suggesting that they may provide a particularly strong stimulus for the body's bone-building processes.

More conventional activities generally produced smaller responses. Walking, step aerobics, and standard resistance workouts performed in the gym were less effective at stimulating the measured indicators of bone formation.

The findings were especially unexpected for resistance training, which is commonly recommended as a way to support skeletal health.

"The most surprising finding was that resistance training did not produce a significant effect on markers of bone metabolism, even though several professional guidelines recommend this type of exercise for maintaining bone health. Likewise, low- or moderate-intensity endurance exercise, such as walking or jogging, showed no meaningful long-term effect," explained Viktória Barna, PhD student at Semmelweis University and first author of the study.

Why Walking and Weight Training Still Matter

The results do not suggest that walking, jogging, or other less demanding activities should be abandoned. These forms of exercise continue to offer important health benefits, even if they do not stimulate the measured bone-building processes as strongly as more intense sports.

Rather, the research indicates that maintaining healthy bones may require greater mechanical stimulation than many everyday activities provide. Movements that place more substantial forces on the skeleton appear to produce a stronger response in the biological processes involved in forming new bone.

However, the researchers stress that people should not suddenly begin strenuous exercise without preparing appropriately.

This is especially important for individuals with cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, or metabolic conditions, as well as those who already have osteoporosis. Anyone in these groups who is considering a new activity or a more physically demanding exercise routine should first speak with their treating physician, general practitioner, or a sports medicine specialist. Medical guidance can help determine whether the activity and its intensity are suitable for their health and physical capabilities.

Could High-Intensity Exercise Help Prevent Osteoporosis?

The findings offer a new perspective on how exercise could be used to maintain bone health as people age. While the analysis focused on markers of bone metabolism rather than direct changes in bone density, the results suggest that vigorous activity may encourage early biological changes that support bone formation.

"According to the World Health Organization, regular physical activity offers numerous health benefits. However, our findings suggest that low-intensity exercise alone is not sufficient to stimulate bone metabolism. High-intensity exercise may trigger early beneficial changes in bone formation, potentially helping to slow bone loss and support healthy aging," summarized Dr. Nóra Sydó, clinical specialist and co-author of the study.

The researchers believe that understanding which movements most effectively stimulate bone formation could lead to better exercise programs designed to preserve skeletal strength and help prevent osteoporosis.

For now, the findings highlight an important distinction: staying physically active is beneficial for overall health, but keeping bones healthy over the long term may depend not only on how much people move, but also on how powerfully and dynamically they move.

Materials provided by Semmelweis University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4330. Battlefield 6 streamlines some of the most annoying Challenges yet again, takes out a few of them entirely

The easier and more accessible Battlefield Studios makes those Battlefield 6 Challenges, the better.

The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done. Having just released a new patch - which already included several updates to Challenges and Assignments - Battlefield Studios has gone in and made even more changes.

This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.

The updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge. Now, any headshot beyond 75m will count. Recon Expert 3 is another headshot-themed one that’s been updated, and now requires getting headshot kills beyond 125m, rather than the practically impossible beyond 200m that it required previously.

The Rapid Fire 2 Challenge, which required getting kills beyond 50m with Assault Rifles, has been changed so it now tracks anything beyond 40m. The painful ‘Inflict damage under 15m while hip-firing with Assault Rifles’ has been entirely replaced with one that requires - the far more sensible - inflicting damage while in ADS with Assault Rifles.

A couple of Challenges, such as the one that required suppressing enemies with LMGs, and another that wanted you to deal damage to laser-designated vehicles using lock-on weapons, have both been removed.

The journey to make Challenges and Assignments easier to complete has been a long one. Progression has been one of the key areas of criticism Battlefield 6 received at launch. The issue encompassed more than just slow player and weapon XP earn rates, it also prevented players from accessing new Training Paths for the various classes, and several of the game's weapons.

Battlefield Studios attacked the problem from multiple angles, initially boosting the XP players and their weapons would earn, before later reducing the requirements of the Challenges themselves. The developer continued to streamline those requirements over multiple patches, including majorly overhauling the system earlier this month.

It seems the studio is more confident than ever in the game, as it recently announced that Battlefield 6 will be getting its first free trial next week, offering players who do not own the full game access to iconic modes like Conquest, and Breakthrough - though on an unusual selection of maps.

Arc Raiders has received a new update today that’s almost entirely dedicated to balance and economy tweaks. Patch 1.3.0 arrived earlier across all platforms, coming in at just under 1GB. This is an especially interesting patch because many of the changes it makes can be seen as a response to player behaviour on Stella Montis, the game’s latest map, which just joined the roster last week.

The weapon is especially powerful when fully-upgraded, something Arc Raiders developer Embark said pushed it beyond what had been originally intended.

In today’s update, the Venator's fire rate is the thing getting hit the hardest, with each upgrade now offering slower gains to the weapon's rate-of-fire compared to the way things were. The weapon’s weight is also being increased to five from two.

Another powerful item players have been getting a lot of mileage out of recently has been the Deadline mine. Unlike the Venator, the Deadline is mainly a threat to Arc enemies, and it’s proven incredibly powerful against the largest and most fearsome, such as the Bastion, and Leaper. In fact, the mine was considered essential when taking down a Queen.

The patch vastly increases its purchase price, and makes it more difficult to craft by upping the amount each of its components requires. Perhaps the most effective nerf, however, is the reduction to the Deadline’s stock at traders from three to just one, which means you’re going to be seeing a lot less of it topside.

Beyond those specific changes, Embark has also tweaked explosive damage across the board. According to the developer, explosive damage was being applied to multiple parts at once, which trivialised some encounters.

This change mainly affects larger Arc units, such as the Bastion, allowing them to withstand more explosive damage before bits start coming off of them. The Hullcracker, one of the best explosive damage weapons, has also caught a nerf as part of that.

#4326. Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. New research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline

To investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

The results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

"This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy said. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The new analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

Murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect."

This effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

"I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed."

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49

One of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy said.

But increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

The research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations

The growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

This increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

"There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy said. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well."

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

Murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

The researchers then plan to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce important features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as new registry information becomes available each year.

Murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

Current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

She also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

The research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

Along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, new cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

#4324. Battlefield 6 may have actually done it: beaten Call of Duty

Battlefield 6 sales are setting all kinds of records, but one in particular has long eluded the Battlefield series.

If you’ve been paying any attention to the shooter market these past few months, you won’t be surprised to learn that Battlefield 6 has been an unprecedented success for EA, and the Battlefield series as a whole.

The game managed to sell over 7 million units at launch, climbing to the top of the charts anywhere you look, including setting new series concurrent player records on Steam. Thanks to new data, we now better understand the true scale of this launch.

The latest Circana report, which looks at game and hardware sales in the United States, has arrived. This iteration covers the month of October, which is when Battlefield 6 was released.

Battlefield 6 was the top-selling game across all platforms during October - which isn’t surprising. It has overtaken NBA 2K26 to become 2025’s best-selling game year-to-date, making it the best-selling Battlefield game ever.

In October alone, the game sold more than the lifetime sales of Battlefield 1, previously the best-selling entry in the franchise.

Battlefield 6 even set records beyond just its own series, having now produced the highest single-month dollar sales (physical and digital) total for any full game released in the last three years. The previous record holder was 2022’s Modern Warfare 2.

November’s report, which is set to arrive midway through December, will show, once and for all, whether Battlefield 6 has been able to overtake Black Ops 7. With one exception, Call of Duty games have, for more than a decade, topped the best-selling year-to-date chart. Regardless of the quality of the individual titles, or the competition in any given year, nothing has been able to shake that dominance.

Given all this momentum, Battlefield 6 has a shot at dethroning Call of Duty this year, beating Black Ops 7 to become the year’s best-seller. You never want to count out the sheer popularity of Call of Duty among casual players, however, which is what’s going to make December’s report all the more interesting.

#4322. PUBG's extraction shooter spin-off, Black Budget, is finally going to be playable next month

The most interesting development in the PUBG universe, PUBG: Black Budget, is almost ready to show itself off to a wider group of players.

You’d be forgiven for not remembering PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction off-shoot of the original battle royale shooter, PUBG. Black Budget has been sort of floating around the internet for months, but Krafton never really committed to revealing core details about the game, or when players will actually get to play it.

This changes today, as the publisher - along with the game’s developer, PUBG Studios, have finally lifted the lid off the upcoming shooter.

Black Budget is described as a “tactical” extraction shooter. Squads of players infiltrate a mysterious island trapped in a time loop. There’s a bit of a STALKER element here with anomalies and various, unpredictable environmental shifts.

Coli, the island in question, hides a research facility that holds secrets and artefacts, which is what players will be attempting to extract. This is very much a PvPvE shooter, though PUBG Studios says the focus will be on exploration and discovery, rather than constant combat.

The game’s first set of closed alpha tests is set for December. The first takes place December 12-14, and another is scheduled for December 19-21. That’s six days across two weeks, with the test only being available on PC. Both sessions will be open to players in North America, Europe, and Asia.

As it usually works with these sorts of tets on Steam, the game’s Steam page has a link where you can request access. If granted, you’ll be able to find the closed alpha in your library and download it when the time comes.

Though this is a closed test, Krafton confirmed that players will be able to capture and livestream their gameplay. In fact, watching content creators might be how you get access, as Black Budget is going to have a Twitch Drops event running alongside those sessions.

When I played Arc Raiders prior to its launch, I likened its tense and uncertain atmosphere to that of the early days of PUBG, so it’s going to be very interesting to see what actual PUBG does with the extraction shooter premise.

So far, it sounds like it’s going to be doing its own thing, leaning more into the adventure side of the subgenre, but we’ll have to see how it all shakes out when the tests start. Indeed, the BR-like constantly shrinking circle sounds like it could be a game-changing twist.

#4319. Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns

To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

Meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

Despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

The highly-anticipated Durin is at last the new playable character. A 5-Star Pyro Sword wielder, Durin can switch between two different forms: one lets him deal damage, while the other is best suited to supporting the team.

Durin was once a dragon, you see, who was later given a human body. This is why he’s able to switch forms. The more powerful, Abyssal-infused form can launch major attacks on single targets to boost his own Vaporize and Melt damage, while his support form reduces enemies’ Elemental Resistance and deals AoE Pyro damage.

Durin’s Story Quest will shed more light on that aspect of his life, and completing it earns you a reward for him. Speaking of quests, completing the Archon Quest will grant you 500 Primogems. All characters connected to the Hexenzirkel can benefit from certain story quests tied to their abilities. This is a big new addition, and will affect Venti, Klee, Albedo, Mona, Razor, Fischl, and Sucrose - all of whom can become Hexerei characters. This ties into the new Hexerei Secret Rite effect, which will trigger when two or more Hexerei characters are present. The effect boosts the entire party’s combat effectiveness.

The other new character in Luna 3 is Jahoda, a 4-Star Anemo Bow wielder who’s great at healing teammates and absorbing Elements, which she can then use to deal damage. The first phase of Luna 3 will feature Durin and Jahoda, alongside the return of Venti. The second phase sees no new character debuts, but does feature the return of Varesa and Xilonen.

There’s more to get excited about in Luna 3, even if you don’t feel like spending most of your time in Nod-Krai. The Soulblazers' Snowbound Journey event will take you back to Dragonspine, where you’ll find winter-theme minigames appropriate to an update cycle spanning December to January. This is how you can earn the 4-Star Rainbow Serpent's Rain Bow, too.

Beyond that, you can also look forward to the Miliastra Wonderland UGC module getting new updates. The Wonderland Resource Center is where creators can get and share resources through the editing tool.

This is the first trial for the core game, and it arrives some six weeks after Battlefield 6 officialy launched, and four weeks following the release of the free-to-play Battlefield Redsec, which has battle royale and other components.

Beyond all the drama surrounding the two rival shooter franchises, the Battlefield 6 trial is itself pretty straightfoward, and is notably nowhere near as genrous as some of the Call of Duty ones we’ve seen recently.

The trial goes live today at 4am PT, 7am ET, 12pm GMT across all platforms, and will be available for a week; ending Tuesday, December 2. It includes three core maps: Siege of Cairo, Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields.

Hopefully EA can resolve this issue before the trial officially kicks off.

#4313. A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy

A promising new approach to building computer chips could dramatically reduce the energy needed for computing, including the rapidly growing demands of artificial intelligence. At the center of the breakthrough is a special class of materials known as multiferroics, which combine electrical and magnetic properties that can be controlled together using extremely small voltages.

These materials could make future electronics far more energy efficient than today's technology. However, a major obstacle has prevented their use in conventional computer chips. When multiferroics are made thin enough to fit inside these devices, they typically lose the electrical and magnetic behavior that makes them valuable. Scientists call this problem the "dead layer" effect.

Researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces extremely thin films of bismuth ferrite, a widely studied multiferroic material, without sacrificing its essential properties. Even more remarkably, the process gives the material new magnetic characteristics that could make it especially useful for future electronics.

"We've established that we can get rid of the dead layer," said Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. "We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want -- down to a few angstroms -- and it's still ferroelectric, and it's still magnetic."

The findings were published in the journal Nature Materials.

Why Multiferroics Could Transform Computer Chips

What makes multiferroics so attractive for computing is the unusual connection between their electrical and magnetic properties. Their atomic structure is made up of repeating units in which positive and negative charges are positioned on opposite sides, creating a property known as electrical polarization.

Applying a small voltage can reverse this polarization, effectively switching the positions of the positive and negative charges. This provides a potential way to store digital information as binary values (ones and zeros) using very little electricity.

Because the material's magnetic behavior is linked to its electrical polarization, the stored information can also be retrieved magnetically. This combination could enable computer memory and logic components that require significantly less energy than existing technologies.

The challenge has been making these materials small enough for practical devices. Modern computer chips require exceptionally thin layers, but multiferroics traditionally stop functioning properly when reduced to such dimensions.

Two separate effects cause this breakdown. First, the material's atomic structure becomes distorted, disrupting the arrangement and chemical environment necessary for its properties to function. Second, internal electric fields interfere with the material's polarization until it can no longer be maintained. Together, these effects destroy both its ferroelectric and magnetic behavior, creating the troublesome dead layer.

How Brown Engineers Eliminated the Dead Layer

To solve the problem, the Brown University team developed a new method for producing thin films of bismuth ferrite.

The researchers deposited the material onto a foundation made of dysprosium scandate, a compound derived from rare earth elements. This underlying material has a crystal structure with slightly smaller dimensions than bismuth ferrite, creating a mismatch between their atomic arrangements.

That mismatch places the bismuth ferrite under compression, helping preserve the atomic structure required for its electrical and magnetic properties to remain intact.

The team also incorporated a second metallic layer designed to counteract unwanted electric fields. By preventing those fields from disrupting the material's electrical polarization, the additional layer addresses the other major cause of the dead layer effect.

Together, these changes allow the bismuth ferrite film to retain its multiferroic properties even when reduced to just a few angstroms in thickness.

But the researchers discovered something else. Rather than simply preserving the material's original capabilities, their approach actually improved its magnetic behavior.

The engineered layers caused the bismuth ferrite to exhibit altermagnetism, an unusual form of magnetism that combines useful characteristics of two more familiar magnetic states: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.

This discovery could be particularly important for developing faster and more compact computer components.

"Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out," Caretta said. "The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds -- they can be fast, densely integrated and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout."

In other words, altermagnets offer a potentially valuable combination of speed, compactness, and readable signals. These characteristics could help engineers build computer components that operate efficiently without the interference problems associated with conventional magnetic materials.

The ability to create this magnetic behavior in an exceptionally thin multiferroic film makes the discovery especially promising for future chip designs.

A New Path Toward Energy-Efficient AI Computing

As artificial intelligence continues to drive demand for computing power, developing hardware that consumes less electricity has become an increasingly important goal.

Caretta believes the new findings could help bring multiferroic materials closer to practical use in low-power memory and computing devices. Although the technology still needs further development before it can be incorporated into commercial chips, the research demonstrates that a long-standing materials limitation can be overcome.

It also shows that carefully engineering a material's atomic environment can do more than preserve its existing properties. Under the right conditions, it can produce useful behavior that was not present in the original material.

"We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials," Caretta said. "The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that's useful -- and sometimes even better than what nature gives us."

The research received funding from the U.S. Army Research Office (W911NF-21-2-0162), the National Science Foundation (DMR-2039380, OIA-2327352) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-AC02-05CH11231).

Materials provided by Brown University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4307. XBOX CEO Casually Reveals Wolfenstein 3 In Production

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

The XBOX brand, through its various acquisitions, has managed to obtain ownership of some of the oldest, arguably most important video game IPs. One of those IPs is Wolfenstein, the series that gave us the first true FPS with the release of Wolfenstein 3D all the way back in 1992. Since 2014, the Wolfenstein IP has been in the hands of MachineGames, with Bethesda serving as publisher. Microsoft owns ZeniMax, Zennimax owns Bethesda, and so XBOX usually gets first dibs when Wolfenstein comes knocking.

You might not think it, but a serious shooter like Wolfenstein 3D was a huge influence, according to Randy Pitchford.

It’s rather fitting, then, that someone high up the chain of command in XBOX would have the privilege of divulging new Wolfenstein news. Though, even then, I certainly wouldn’t expect the someone in question to be its literal CEO, nor would I expect said news to drop on a random Thursday, but let nobody say they can’t make things interesting.

On her personal X, formerly Twitter account, XBOX CEO Asha Sharma rather casually announced that MachineGames has officially begun production on the next mainline Wolfenstein game, the first since Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus was released in 2017. Obviously, since production has just started, details are basically non-existent, but both Sharma and MachineGames’ own X account did give us a couple of tidbits to chew on.

Sharma’s tweet keeps the announcement fairly quick and concise, reading, “Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at @MachineGames. One of gaming's most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more.”

One of gaming's most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward.

Assuming the game will have some manner of subtitle like its predecessors, Sharma didn’t divulge what it was. What she did share, though, was a screenshot of the game’s apparent script. This screenshot is apparently set during the game’s first chapter in a locale called “Nazitraz,” presumably a prison of some sort, in which series protagonist B.J. Blazkowicz confronts a man named “Otto,” who blubbers in fear in his presence. Series mainstay Fergus Reid also appears to be present, but the screenshot cuts off before he says or does anything.

The Elder Scrolls 6 has finally had its title officially confirmed, weeks after it was not so subtly leaked to the wider public.

Shortly after Sharma’s tweet, MachineGames shared the same script screenshot on its own X account alongside the caption, “His reputation precedes him. Wolfenstein 3 is in production.” MachineGames’ post also added a photo of two actors in the midst of motion-capture work: Debra Wilson, who previously played Grace Walker in New Colossus, and B.J.’s actor, Brian Bloom.

Wolfenstein, as a series, has been pretty quiet for a few years now. As I mentioned, New Colossus was the last mainline game to release, which was nearly a decade ago in 2017. The series has had spin-offs since then, including Wolfenstein: Youngblood and Wolfenstein: Cyberpilot, both of which were released in 2019. The former was a co-op game starring B.J.’s teenage daughters as they searched for their father in France, while the latter was a VR game in which an unnamed hacker works to hack various Nazi robots. Unfortunately, neither of these games were particularly well-received.

Still, there’s no reason to be pessimistic, especially considering that it was MachineGames that brought us the unexpected slam dunk that was Indiana Jones and the Great Circle in 2024. I’d say that’s pretty definitive proof that the studio still knows how to put an excellent game together, and I’m optimistic about what’s on the horizon.

Incidentally, MachineGames is also involved in a creative capacity for the live-action Wolfenstein series that’s currently in development for Prime Video. Who knows, we might just have a one-two punch of new Wolfenstein media to look forward to in the not-too-distant future.

MachineGames is making sure the Indiana Jones DLC is challenging, no matter how many hours you've put into the base game.
