#4260. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 30, 2026

Welcome to Devil's Night, the night before Halloween, where video games are best served scary. After tomorrow night – Halloween proper – no more scary video games allowed. At least not until mid-September, 2027. I'm sorry, I don't make the rules. Below you will find our weekend gaming recommendations (which is actually surprisingly light on scary games – apologies), but before that, here are some of the biggest stories of the week.

Phantom Blade Zero is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, and it’s certainly one of the most impressive to watch. Beijing-based developer S-Game uses China’s Wuxia brand of action (which was actually banned for some time during the 20th Century by the country’s government) to create a stylish, fluid, and hyper-engaging combat system. It will constantly leave you in awe that action combat can look this good. But looks aren’t everything. Fortunately, Phantom Blade Zero delivers on all fronts, with weapon mechanics so detailed that picking up a new blade can feel like unlocking a new character in a fighting game. The story won’t blow your socks off, but it’s certainly engaging and enticing enough to bring you through Phantom Blade Zero’s 40 or so hours of content. If you’re not interested in the “perfect ending,” which is the only satisfactory one in my opinion, you can complete the game in less than 30 hours. S-Game mixes high-octane combat with sprawling and rewarding exploration to create a must-play during this already busy season of games. You can read more of my thoughts in the Game Informer Phantom Blade Zero review, and if you are hopping in this weekend, be sure to check out my list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks I wish I knew before starting it.

If you have any fond memories of IllFonic’s ill-fated Friday the 13th: The Game as I do, you simply must play the studio’s latest, Halloween: The Game. It is essentially Friday the 13th with Michael Myers instead of Jason, but with a decade of lessons learned from the team’s teeth carving in other horror properties and games. You’re either Michael or a citizen; the former wants to kill you and all the NPCs in various suburban maps, while the latter must rescue as many NPCs as possible while staying alive themselves. It’s that classic cat-and-mouse formula IllFonic is the master of, but with all the style, substance, and synths of John Carpenter’s Halloween masterpiece. Plus, Halloween: The Game features IllFonic’s first crack at a single-player campaign, and while it’s largely a tutorial for playing as Michael, if you’re a Halloween mega-fan like me, it’s worth checking out if only to take part in some of the film’s most iconic kills. You can read more of my thoughts in the Game Informer Halloween: The Game review here, and if you’re hopping in this weekend, there’s a new map, additional Halloween-themed cosmetics to unlock, and more waiting for you.

Overwatch is in the midst of its Halloween event, which have always historically been pretty interesting. This year it's Mystery Madness: Graveyard Games. In it, you begin by picking one of three characters in a random role. And then, as the game progresses, you choose perks that upgrade, alter, or completely change what your character can do. It can get really chaotic where by round three characters like Orisa might be three times her normal size or Torbjorn might have placed a giant turret on Mercy's making her a flying death machine. There are also Halloween skins, as well.

Tom the Postgirl is an odd little adventure that I'd recommend to fans of Untitled Goose Game. You play as Tom, a creepy girl who's tasked with delivering packages to the people of her wacky town, which is depicted with storybook-style illustrations and a color palette limited to black, white, and red. On the surface, you're delivering packages, but the game's real story is based on Tom's tendency to peep where she shouldn't, peering into townsfolks' windows to watch their odd lives. On house is full of kids who live like dogs; another has a couple with a bizarre obsession with tickling. You never know what each window might reveal, and I quickly sympathized with (and enabled) Tom's compulsion. You also have the capacity to cause quite a bit of trouble by stomping on flowers, haphazardly snipping strings and cords, or even stealing packages and using them for your own mischievous purposes. It's a pretty short experience, completable in just a few hours, making it a nice palate cleanser between the massive releases at the end of the year.

This Devolver Digital-published game has a simple but head-turning premise. You’re a profoundly angry woman who returns to her small hometown armed with nothing but a sledgehammer, which she uses to smash everything in sight. The town is also inhabited by robots possessing human consciousnesses. Swinging the hammer can either punch holes through walls or, with enough force, reduce entire buildings to rubble. But why is she doing this? Why is she so mad? A big part of Virtue and a Sledgehammer’s allure is its fascinating and well-written tale about the protagonist’s strained relationships with her sister and mother. Learning more about their lives requires you to keep smashing, but the more you learn, the more you begin to question whether smashing everything is actually a good idea.

This bizarre indie blends fun match-3 puzzle-solving with tower defense gameplay wrapped around a funny but surreal story. The match-3 gameplay involves sliding tiles to match geographic elements like castles, trees, and rivers to collect resources that feed into the tower defense portion. Depending on how the board looks when the puzzle portion ends, you send troops (sustained by the resources you collected) to attack/defend against rival castles and gather more items; board positioning determines how well this can go. The two mechanics feed into each other to create a fun loop that grows in complexity as new mechanics are introduced. Did I mention the game is also very weird? The silly tale centers on a medieval court designating you the chosen savior to rescue their lost queen (and many other tasks), and the dumb tone adds personality to a sometimes dry genre. Titanium Court charmed and impressed us when it launched on PC earlier this year, and now console and mobile players get their chance to hold court.

Sword of the Sea is a beautiful, 2025 game about surfing through the sand atop a floating sword. It recalls Journey, the emotional 2012 PlayStation game, which makes sense as it comes from the artists and developers that worked on that game, developer Giant Squid. Giant Squid also made 2016's Abzû and 2020's The Pathless. It's a talented team and Sword of the Sea maintains that reputation. And now you can play it on Switch 2. You can read my full review of the game (though this review pertains to the PlayStation 5 version) right here.

Cities: Skylines arrived on PC more than a decade ago, but is still revered as one of the greatest modern city-builders. Even now, three years after the sequel's release, Paradox continues supporting and porting the original game. A couple years after its initial release, Cities: Skylines received a strong console port, which did an admirable job of adapting the controls to gamepads, but the Switch version was always the weakest of the bunch. As of this week, Switch 2 owners can play a less compromised version, expanding the Switch's 9-tile limit to a much larger 25-tile limit, as well as better performance and textures, better control panels, and a ton of DLC and added content. And on top of that, if you own the Switch 1 version, you get a deep discount on the Switch 2 version.

While not specifically about this new Switch 2 version, you can read our original reviews of the base PC version here, and the base console version here.

Minecraft has held its dominant spot in pop culture for so long that it's easy to forget a simple fact about it: the game is awesome. This week, it's coming to Switch 2, giving potential miners another platform to explore procedurally-generated caves in. You've certainly heard of it, and you've probably played it, but I still feel it often doesn't get the flowers it deserves in high-level critical discussions about games, despite its regular cadence of major updates. The opening gameplay loop is so satisfying that for many of my peers, whether they regularly play video games or not, it's only a matter of time before they boot up a new world again. While you can never play the game for the first time again, if you haven't checked it out in a couple years, you might be surprised by the amount of new blocks, materials, and mobs they've added in recent updates. And if you've never played before, the Switch 2 launch is as good a time as any to see what all the fuss is about.

The card game incarnation of Arkham Horror remains one of the best narrative-driven and horror-themed tabletop games around, and it's an easy recommendation if you're looking for something engaging to dive into on Halloween night. Rooted in the monsters and mysteries of the Cthulhu Mythos, this living card game is built on major core sets and expansions. But unlike a TCG, each new installment has the same cards included, fueling the cooperative adventures you'll undertake together with your fellow players. Last year Arkham Horror: The Card Game did something of a soft relaunch for a chapter 2 of its narrative, and that new core set is an ideal place to jump on  play. Players each control an individual investigator as they explore arcane and weird mysteries, confront monsters, and unfold plots of cultists, ancient entities, and forbidden lore. For fans of cosmic horror storytelling, it's an easy pick.

#4258. A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math

For some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates. Even when they practice and receive instruction, they may continue to struggle with problems that other children their age can solve more easily. Researchers are now uncovering clues about why these difficulties persist, and the answers may involve more than an understanding of numbers.

One possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems. A new study from Stanford University suggests that children with persistent math difficulties may have trouble adjusting their approach when faced with different mathematical challenges. The researchers also identified distinctive patterns of brain activity associated with these struggles.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University. Their work focused on children with a condition that causes ongoing difficulty with mathematical problem solving (developmental dyscalculia). Although the condition has been recognized for years, scientists are still working to understand the specific thinking processes and brain mechanisms that contribute to it.

Why Some Children Struggle With Math Strategies

To investigate these challenges, the Stanford team studied 68 children between the ages of 8 and 10. They examined how the children approached math problems, how effectively they used different strategies, and how their brain activity related to their performance.

Solving a math problem often requires more than knowing numbers or remembering arithmetic facts. Children must also decide which approach will work best. For example, a child might count individual numbers to find an answer or use a more efficient method based on a familiar mathematical relationship. As problems become more difficult, the ability to recognize when a different strategy is needed can become increasingly important.

The researchers found that children with developmental dyscalculia were generally less effective at using different mathematical strategies than children without the condition. They took longer to shift from one method to another and were less responsive when the difficulty of a problem changed.

Another important difference involved learning to choose better strategies over time. While other children became more effective at selecting appropriate approaches, those with developmental dyscalculia did not show the same improvement. This suggests that their difficulties may involve not only performing calculations but also deciding how to approach a problem in the first place.

Brain Activity Reveals New Clues to Math Difficulties

The researchers also examined patterns of brain activity to better understand what might be happening behind these behavioral differences.

They discovered that activity within a particular brain system differed between children with developmental dyscalculia and those who were more skilled at selecting and using math strategies. These neural patterns were not simply unrelated differences. They could also predict how effectively children counted and how well they switched between approaches when solving problems.

The findings highlight the possible importance of several mental abilities that extend beyond mathematics itself. These include attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to adjust thinking or behavior when circumstances change.

Such abilities are part of what researchers often call executive functions. These mental processes help people organize information, stay focused on a task, hold relevant details in mind, and change plans when an approach is not working. In mathematics, they can help a child keep track of numbers, compare possible solutions, and recognize when to try a different method.

The Stanford findings suggest that difficulties involving these processes may contribute to the development of dyscalculia. Differences in brain activity may also help explain why some children have persistent trouble choosing and changing problem-solving strategies.

However, the observed connections do not establish that the brain activity differences directly cause the condition. They provide new evidence about the cognitive and neural processes associated with these mathematical difficulties.

Understanding Why Math Struggles Differ Between Children

An important conclusion is that developmental dyscalculia does not appear to involve one simple problem shared by every affected child. Instead, different children may experience difficulties involving several interacting mental processes.

As Lasnick explains, "Importantly, this study also emphasizes the individual variability observed in dyscalculia, further demonstrating that the disorder reflects cognitive and neural dysfunction across multiple processes."

By connecting children's mathematical behavior with measurable differences in brain activity, the research offers a more detailed picture of why math can be persistently challenging for some students.

The findings also point toward the importance of looking beyond whether a child gets the correct answer. Understanding how children choose strategies, adapt to more difficult problems, and manage the mental demands of mathematics could ultimately help researchers develop better ways to identify and support those with developmental dyscalculia.

#4257. Genshin Impact Version Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, including the long-awaited Moon Maiden Columbina

The first major Genshin Impact update in 2026 is almost here, bringing characters we've been waiting a while to play, and more besides.

Genshin Impact’s latest Special Program has spilled all the beans on the game’s next major update, Luna 4. The update, which arrives on January 14, kicks off 2026 with several bits of new content, including some previously-teased characters.

Dubbed Traveler on a Winter's Night, Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, and brings back The Lantern Rite event to celebrate the beginning of the new year.

The first new arrival in Version Luna 4 is Columbina Hyposelenia, the Moon Maiden. Columbina is a 5-Star Hydro Catalyst wielder. Her kit revolves around supporting the squad via Lunar Reactions. She can trigger coordinated Lunar Reaction DMG, even when she’s off the field.

The Moon Maiden’s special ability, Lunar Domain, further boosts all Lunar Reactions by applying a DMG bonus, including summoning more thundercloud strikes for Lunar-Charged reactions. Columbina is also capable of converting Electro-Charged, Bloom, and Hydro Crystallize reactions into Lunar Reactions, as well as revive fallen squad members.

Speaking of elemental reactions, new in this version is Lunar-Crystallize, a new reaction that’s triggered when Geo meets Hydro (under certain conditions). When triggered, Lunar-Crystallize summons three Moondrifts near enemies. When triggered three times, Moondrift Harmony gets activated, dealing Geo DMG to enemies caught in its radius.

Then there’s Zibai, an Adeptus from Liyue. Zibai is another 5-Star character, a Geo Sword wielder. Zibai can, through entering a special state where they can build up energy, unleash an Elemental Skill that deals Lunar-Crystallize DMG.

The longer the fight goes on, the more Lunar-Crystallize reactions are triggered, the higher (and more often) the damage of Zibai’s Elemental Skill becomes.

Luna 4 continues the Nod-Krai story arc, with a big confrontation with Il Dottore. This is the focus of the new Archon Quest, completing which will earn you a new outfit. There’s a gameplay element to that new chapter, too, with the reveal of Piramida, a new area north of the region. Piramida is the headquarters of the Lightkeepers.

#4252. Nintendo May Have Just Teased a Beloved Zelda Game Coming to Switch Online

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

It's been a little over a week since the release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, but Zelda fans are already hungry for more (and I include myself there!).

And while Nintendo hasn't announced another major release for the franchise just yet, a curious discovery on the company's official website has sparked speculation that one beloved adventure could finally be making its way to Nintendo Switch Online.

Following the remake’s launch, Nintendo recently launched a new section on Nintendo.com dedicated to the full catalog of games in The Legend of Zelda franchise.

Called “Game History”, the page lists the series' entries in release order, allowing visitors to explore the history of Hyrule and see which platforms each adventure originally launched on. You can also sort and filter the games however you like, and there's even a lovely little feature that shows how old you were when each Zelda game came out!

Nintendo has announced that the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time became the fastest selling Switch 2 game in under a week.

However, the most interesting detail is that Nintendo's website also indicates which games are playable through Nintendo Switch Online. And that's where things get a little strange.

As spotted by fans on Reddit, The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds is currently listed as playable with Nintendo Switch Online on the official website. That's particularly interesting because the 2013 adventure was originally released for the Nintendo 3DS and isn't currently available through the subscription service.

As spotted by fans on Reddit, The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds is currently listed as playable with Nintendo Switch Online on the official website.

Naturally, this has led some players to believe Nintendo might be preparing to bring the beloved handheld classic to modern platforms and just let that accidentally slip! But I gotta say, A Link Between Worlds is widely regarded as one of the standout entries in the franchise, and its unique mechanic of allowing Link to transform into a painting and move along walls would definitely make for a welcome addition to the Switch Online library.

The first gameplay trailer for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has confirmed that it has added a beloved feature from the 3DS version.

Still, not everyone is convinced this is an intentional tease. Some players believe the listing is simply a website error that Nintendo will eventually correct – after all, the company hasn't announced any plans to introduce Nintendo 3DS games to Switch Online, and the service doesn't currently offer a dedicated 3DS game library.

It is important to highlight that, at the time of writing, Nintendo hasn't publicly addressed the listing or announced that A Link Between Worlds is coming to Nintendo Switch Online. And the game is still marked as playable through the service on the official website, but that alone isn't enough to confirm anything!

Of course, this wouldn't be the first time Nintendo fans have found themselves digging through official websites for clues about upcoming releases. And considering how many classic Zelda adventures remain unavailable on modern hardware, it's easy to understand why this particular discovery has generated excitement.

For now, I'd recommend keeping expectations in check! A Link Between Worlds joining Nintendo Switch Online would be fantastic news, but until Nintendo says something officially, this is still firmly in rumor territory. Hopefully, it's a mistake that the company won't be correcting anytime soon.

Some of the original's most charming quirks from Zelda: Ocarina of Time didn't make the journey.

#4250. Diablo 4's long-awaited Tower and its Leaderboards enter beta today, and there's no PTR funny business this time

Diablo 4's first big moment of 2026 is nearly upon us, and it's one feature many have been looking forward to for actual years.

Diablo 4 is about to deliver on Blizzard’s years-old promise to add a challenging, leaderboard-driven experience to the action RPG. The beta for The Tower, and its associated Leaderboards are about to kick off.

As recently revealed, the new experience launches today at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT. This is a beta version that arrives alongside update 2.5.2.

This early launch won’t offer the full experience, and it’s mainly designed to get it into the hands of players early so that Blizzard could get as much feedback as possible and incorporate it into the final version.

The beta is available to everyone, which is a nice change from the usual rigmarole players would have to go through to get the PTR build and play on a different branch. The Tower, and Leaderboards will be available only in the Seasonal Realm, however. Indeed, the plan is to build on what’s there with each future season, so it’s best to think of it as a seasonal experience.

The Tower is about as simple of an activity as you can get in an action RPG. The goal is to climb as many floors as you can as quickly as you can, all while battling increasingly difficult mobs.

You need to reach and beat the Tower’s final boss before you can call it a run. The Leaderboard will then show your time, and let you see how well you did compared to other players.

The Tower is available to anyone who completed Rank 2 of the current Season Rank. Once done, an Obelisk will appear in Cerrigar, letting you access the challenge.

The Leaderboards themselves will operate on a two-week schedule, all of which will take place during a given season. In this case, they’re going to close the day before Season of the Divine Interversion - the game’s current season - ends.

Blizzard published an updated set of patch notes that show how much has changed since The Tower, and Leaderboards first became playable in the patch 2.5.0 PTR.

Though the two new additions have been anticipated for a while, there’s not been much exciting going on in the world of Diablo 4, apart, of course, from the surprise arrival of The Paladin class, which became available in December last year to coincide with the announcement of Lord of Hatred, the game’s next expansion.

#4248. Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel

Used coffee grounds may be far more valuable than they appear. Instead of ending up in the trash, this everyday waste could provide ingredients for renewable fuels and a variety of useful chemicals. Researchers at Universitat Rovira i Virgili (URV) have identified an efficient way to recover oil from discarded coffee grounds while keeping the remaining material suitable for other industrial applications.

The findings, published in Biomass and Bioenergy, highlight the untapped potential of spent coffee grounds, a waste product generated in enormous quantities worldwide. Global coffee bean production reaches approximately 10 million metric tons annually, but only a small fraction of the beans' material makes its way into the brewed beverage. Much of the rest is discarded as solid waste. These leftover grounds contain roughly 15% lipids, or fats, which can serve as ingredients for producing biodiesel.

Finding a More Efficient Way to Extract Oil From Coffee Grounds

To determine how best to recover these valuable oils, researchers Jorge F. Romero, Alberto Tampieri, Daniel Montané, Magdalena Constantí, and Francesc Medina from URV's Department of Chemical Engineering examined three variables: extraction temperature, processing duration, and the amount of solvent used relative to the coffee grounds.

The team used n-hexane, a solvent widely employed to separate fats from other materials. Through a series of carefully designed experiments, they evaluated how changes in temperature, extraction time, and solvent quantity affected the results, both individually and in combination.

"We have found that the optimal conditions are at 45°C for 60 minutes with a ratio of 35 milliliters of hexane per gram of dry residue," explained Magdalena Constantí, one of the study's authors.

Under these conditions, the researchers recovered approximately 90% as much oil as could be extracted using Soxhlet, a standard laboratory method known for its high extraction yields. Although Soxhlet is effective, it generally takes longer, consumes more energy, and is less practical for large industrial operations.

The newer approach also produced considerably cleaner oil. The optimized extraction yielded just 0.3% impurities, compared with 3.9% using Soxhlet. Chemical analysis revealed that the oil's fatty acid composition remained consistent across the different experimental conditions, with linoleic and palmitic acids making up the largest shares. This composition supports the oil's potential use as an ingredient in biodiesel production.

Coffee Waste Could Produce More Than Just Biodiesel

Recovering oil is only one part of the opportunity. The scientists also wanted to ensure that extracting the fats would not destroy the remaining coffee material, which contains compounds that could be used to manufacture additional fuels and chemicals.

"In our study, we also demonstrate that extracting the oil does not mean that the rest of the material cannot be used for something else," pointed out Francesc Medina, a researcher at the Department of Chemical Engineering who participated in the research.

A central goal was to protect the structural components of the leftover coffee grounds, collectively known as the lignocellulosic matrix. This material contains cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, substances that can be processed into products such as bioethanol, lactic acid, polyhydroxyalkanoates, phenolic compounds, and ingredients used to produce sustainable aviation fuels.

Removing the oil may actually make the remaining material easier to process. Fats can form a barrier that prevents solvents and catalysts from reaching other useful components within the plant matter. By extracting the oils without substantially changing the underlying structure, the researchers created a residue better suited for further processing.

In this way, the method serves two purposes. It recovers a potentially valuable source of biodiesel ingredients while preparing the leftover biomass for conversion into other products.

A Simpler Approach to Sustainable Biofuel Production

The team also investigated whether more advanced extraction methods could deliver better results. These included techniques that use ultrasound or microwaves to accelerate oil recovery.

Although both alternatives can speed up the early stages of extraction, neither offered a sufficiently compelling overall improvement. When the researchers considered oil purity, extraction efficiency, energy requirements, and the potential to expand production to an industrial scale, the conventional batch process using n-hexane under moderate conditions emerged as the more balanced option.

That combination of efficiency and practicality could make the method useful in biorefineries, facilities designed to convert biological materials into fuels, chemicals, and other products.

The research also supports the broader goal of creating a circular economy, in which materials that would otherwise be thrown away are reused to generate additional value. This approach is particularly relevant as industries search for renewable fuel alternatives in sectors that are difficult to electrify, including heavy transportation.

By finding ways to make use of both the extracted oils and the remaining coffee grounds, the scientists hope to reduce waste while expanding the range of materials available for sustainable fuel production.

As Daniel Montané, another researcher involved in the study, explained, the goal is "to transform a typically underused waste product into various energy vectors and bio-based chemical products, and to reduce the environmental impact associated with its accumulation."

The findings suggest that discarded coffee grounds could eventually become an important feedstock for producing renewable fuels and other valuable materials, turning a familiar source of everyday waste into a resource with multiple industrial uses.

Materials provided by Universitat Rovira i Virgili. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4246. The Sims developer vows "our values are unchanged," as it teases multiple projects from post-Saudi-owned EA

The team behind one of EA's most diverse franchises has issued a statement about its future under the soon-to-be Saudi-owned publisher.

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

This, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s new ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.)

Some of these projects will see more playtesting throughout 2026, so you should probably sign up for The Sims Labs if you want to hear about when/how you can get involved.

#4243. A new fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome

A specially designed fiber supplement may offer a promising new way to improve gut health for millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Researchers at Edith Cowan University (ECU) have developed and tested a fiber combination that supports beneficial gut bacteria without making common digestive symptoms worse.

The research team at ECU's Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) found that the supplement, called ur gut®, improved gut health in people with IBS without increasing abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.

IBS affects people around the world, including nearly 11 percent of Australians. Although its exact cause remains unclear, stress, infections, and certain medications may contribute to the condition. Symptoms can also become worse because of particular foods, inadequate sleep, psychological stress, hormonal changes, and lifestyle factors.

Why Common IBS Diets Can Affect Gut Health

People with IBS are frequently advised to follow a low-FODMAP diet, which limits certain carbohydrates that are easily fermented by gut bacteria. Although this approach can help control uncomfortable symptoms, restricting these foods may also have unintended consequences for the gut microbiome.

"For years we've known that a diet low in Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monesaccharides and Polyols (FODMAPs) can relieve symptoms, but they can also reduce beneficial gut bacteria and negatively impact fiber intake over time," lead author Dr. Tina Yan said.

"We wanted to find a way to build better gut health while following a low-FODMAP diet."

The new findings suggest that a carefully formulated fiber supplement could help address this problem, allowing people with IBS to support a healthier gut microbiome while continuing to manage their symptoms through dietary changes.

The researchers attribute the supplement's promising effects to its combination of two ingredients: resistant starch and psyllium husk.

Psyllium appears to slow the breakdown of resistant starch by gut bacteria, allowing more of it to reach deeper sections of the colon before fermentation occurs. This process may increase the production of beneficial compounds that support intestinal health.

Ordinarily, fermentable fiber can be challenging for people with IBS because bacterial fermentation can produce excess gas and increase digestive discomfort. The new formulation appears to offer a way to obtain the benefits of fermentation without aggravating these symptoms.

"Traditionally, fermentable fibers can be difficult for people with IBS because they can increase gas production and discomfort," Dr. Yan said.

"What's exciting about this study is that participants maintained stable symptoms while showing meaningful improvements in their gut microbiota as well as in their gut-related anxiety."

Significant Changes in Gut Bacteria and Anxiety

The researchers observed substantial shifts in the composition of participants' gut bacteria during the intervention. These changes were particularly notable because they occurred over a relatively short period.

"Changes of this magnitude are rarely seen with such a short intervention," ur gut® co-creator Professor Amanda Devine said.

"The study demonstrated that our targeted dietary fiber blend positively reshaped the gut microbiome in people with IBS following a low-FODMAP diet, supporting beneficial bacteria linked to gut and mental health. This was great to see."

Alongside improvements in gut bacteria, participants also experienced reductions in gut-related anxiety. These findings suggest that the supplement's potential benefits may extend beyond changes in the digestive system, although further research will be needed to establish its broader effects.

A New Approach to Managing Irritable Bowel Syndrome

The researchers believe their findings could help shift IBS care toward improving the underlying health of the gut rather than focusing exclusively on avoiding foods that cause discomfort.

"For many people with IBS, success has traditionally meant simply avoiding certain foods," ur gut® co-creator Associate Professor Claus Christophersen said.

"Our findings suggest we may also be able to actively rebuild gut health and the microbiome while not making IBS symptoms worse. That's an important step forward."

By demonstrating that beneficial gut bacteria can be supported without increasing IBS symptoms, the study points toward new dietary strategies that could complement existing treatments.

The ur gut® supplement is already available for purchase. The research team has also created a cookbook featuring recipes designed to help people incorporate the supplement into a healthy diet.

The study, "Dietary fibre blend improves gut health in patients with irritable bowel syndrome following a low FODMAP diet: a randomised, double-blind control trial," was published online in the European Journal of Nutrition.

Materials provided by Edith Cowan University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4239. Bobara review - "A lot of waiting around"

Bobara is one of those idle games where you are waiting around and then are delighted when something happens. In Bobara, there is a tiny capybara called Momo who is hanging out inside a Japanese water bath. It's warm there, and he seems cosy.

The app itself tracks your local weather. When it was windy outside, I saw the trees change and whistle away. When it rains, it rains in the game as well. It's a nice touch, seeing the weather change! Beyond that, you can tap various bits of the screen. Momo will give you a few phrases about what they are like and what is happening around him.

You can also change a boba tea at the bottom of the app, which you are meant to do when you have that same tea in real life. There isn't a way for the game to verify this, and instead you can just change it. These sort of lure different creatures or items to Momo, which are held inside your tea house.

Some of the trinkets are food like pretzels and milk bread. They don't appear around Momo. Characters like Cha and Yuki hang out with Momo, and you can tap them as well. Other than that, Bobara doesn't have much else going on. There is no real goal beyond hoping that you end up collecting everything else that the game has to offer. You can use Siri to speak to the app and change your boba via voice command, if you want to put the app on your Apple Watch, which is a nice touch.

At the same time, there just wasn't a lot to keep me interested. I wish that I could interact with my trinkets and could move them about a house or decorate in some way. But, the game is more of a collection and a pet.

#4238. The Elder Scrolls VI Has An Official Subtitle And It's 'Sentinel'

The headline tells the story: The Elder Scrolls VI has an official subtitle and it's Sentinel. So the full game is now titled The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel, or, as we will undoubtedly refer to it moving forward, as we colloquially do with the previous three games (Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim), Sentinel.

The news comes from Bethesda's various social media accounts, which are all sharing the video above. Along with the video, music, and the title, it also shares the text as a quote attributed to Yazar, Moth Priest to High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell (4E 206): "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate."

Sentinel is one of the nine major kingdoms within Hammerfell and is the capital of both the Alik'r Desert region and the Myrkwasa region of the Alik'r (source: elderscrolls.fandom). With this knowledge, it's fair to assume Sentinel will have many desert locations.

The name continues the tradition of naming the games after locations in the Elder Scrolls universe. Oblivion is the sort of exception, as it is a realm, but it still counts. We still don't know exactly when The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel will be released, but we're now about seven years from its original announcement at E3 2018.

#4236. Ocarina of Time Remake Finally Gives Zelda’s Saddest Story the Attention It Deserves

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

After nearly 30 years, the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is finally here, and it's already winning over critics and fans alike – myself included. As I highlighted in my review, this new version embodies what a modern remake should be: an experience that embraces contemporary improvements without losing the old soul of the classic we all love!

And one of the things I've always loved about Ocarina of Time is how many curious characters are scattered throughout Hyrule. Some have surprisingly elaborate backstories, while others barely give you enough information to understand what's going on. More often than not, you need to be genuinely curious to piece together their stories and figure out what they're doing in the world.

My favorite example, by far, is Grog, a rather strange-looking punk who barely appeared in the original game but arguably had one of its saddest stories. Much of what made his character so fascinating came from the lovely fan theories surrounding his family and his mysterious disappearance.

To my surprise, the Switch 2 remake doesn't just subtly address some of those theories, but it also expands Grog's story in ways that make his already tragic arc considerably more meaningful. And to appreciate just how much has changed, we first need to revisit what made this little side story so memorable in the first place.

First things first, let's remember how Grog's story unfolded in the original Ocarina of Time. The character only appeared in two locations throughout the entire adventure: beneath a tree in Kakariko Village at night as Child Link, and later in the Lost Woods as Adult Link.

In Kakariko Village, you'll find him sitting beneath the tree in the center of town, looking rather miserable. Talk to him, and you'll quickly discover that he's not exactly the friendliest person around. He's withdrawn, bitter, and apparently hates just about everyone – including Link, simply for daring to approach him! And that's pretty much all you get from this first encounter.

To my surprise, the Switch 2 remake doesn't just subtly address some of those theories, but it also expands Grog's story in ways that make his already tragic arc considerably more meaningful.

His second appearance, however, is where things get interesting. As Adult Link, you can find Grog in the Lost Woods, but getting him to appear requires a little detour. First, you need to talk to the Cucco Lady in Kakariko Village, who turns out to be Grog's sister. She explains that he had a falling-out with their father, the village's Master Craftsman, and eventually left home. She's worried about him, though, so she gives you an egg that eventually hatches into Cojiro, Grog's beloved blue Cucco.

After using Cojiro to wake up Talon in Kakariko Village, you can take the Cucco into the Lost Woods. That's when you'll finally find Grog again, now seven years later, sitting in a rather strange, almost lifeless state. However, showing him Cojiro seems to snap him out of it, and he asks you to take an Odd Mushroom to the Granny's Potion Shop so she can prepare a medicine for him.

There's just one problem: when you return with the medicine, Grog is nowhere to be found. Instead, you're greeted by Fado, one of the Kokiri children, who explains that he disappeared into the Lost Woods. She also tells you that adults who get lost in the forest turn into Stalfos – those skeletal enemies that have been giving Link a hard time throughout the adventure.

And just like that, Grog's story appears to come to an end. The implication is pretty heartbreaking: the troubled young man who left home after a disagreement with his father has seemingly lost himself in the forest, never to return.

But even that brief story leaves plenty of unanswered questions. What exactly happened between Grog and his father? Why was he so unhappy? And what was the medicine supposed to cure? The original game never gave us definitive answers, leaving players to connect the dots through scattered dialogue and a handful of subtle clues. Thankfully, the remake finally gives us a much closer look at what was going on!

Some of the original's most charming quirks from Zelda: Ocarina of Time didn't make the journey.

One of the most interesting additions in the remake is a new time system that allows the day-night cycle to progress naturally even while you're exploring towns and villages. Outside of more contained areas, such as dungeons and minigame shops, NPCs now follow their own schedules, appearing in different locations and going about their daily routines.

It's a relatively small change, but it makes Hyrule feel considerably more alive – and if you're a fan of Majora's Mask, you'll probably appreciate the familiar feeling of watching characters follow their own little agendas instead of simply standing around waiting for Link to show up!

Outside of more contained areas, such as dungeons and minigame shops, NPCs now follow their own schedules, appearing in different locations and going about their daily routines.

More importantly, this new system gives us additional opportunities to learn about Grog when playing as Child Link. For starters, you can now find him during the day near the entrance to Kakariko Village's graveyard. He's officially identified as the Master Craftsman's Son, making his connection to the village's grumpy carpenter much clearer from the beginning. Talk to him (or simply get close enough to hear him mumbling to himself) and you'll discover that his hatred for practically everything is closely tied to his strained relationship with his father.

And speaking of the Master Craftsman, the remake also gives us a better look at his daily routine. He and his assistants no longer spend all their time repeating the same actions in the same spots. Instead, they're spread throughout the village, and they even gather in front of the central tree for a meeting as the day comes to an end.

Talking to the assistants reveals that they also find their boss rather difficult to deal with. He's a grumpy, demanding man who seems to have a complaint about just about everything. Yet, interestingly enough, none of those complaints ever seem to involve Grog. While his son is clearly consumed by their strained relationship, the Master Craftsman barely acknowledges that anything is wrong – or just wants to ignore it.

But my favorite addition is that you can actually follow Grog around Kakariko Village throughout the day. He eventually gets up from his spot and sneaks behind a pile of bricks near the construction site overseen by his father. There, he quietly mutters that he needs to wait for the Master Craftsman to leave before he can go inside.

And when night finally falls, Grog makes his way back to the central tree, recreating the exact scene we remember from the original game. It's such a small sequence, but it adds an entirely new layer to his character. We no longer just see a miserable young man sitting beneath a tree. We see someone who is actively avoiding his father, seemingly unable to find a way to repair their relationship. And considering what we eventually learn about Grog, that little detail becomes even more heartbreaking.

The remake also expands Grog's story when playing as Adult Link, particularly through additional dialogue with his sister and mother. As in the original, you'll only encounter Grog in the Lost Woods once you reach the point in the Biggoron Sword side quest where Cojiro has turned blue. However, the Cucco Lady now has considerably more information to share about why her brother left home in the first place.

According to her, Grog didn't want to follow the family business. While their father expected him to become a carpenter, Grog wanted to work with animals, something he was particularly passionate about and apparently quite good at. The Master Craftsman strongly disapproved of this decision, and their disagreement eventually caused a complete breakdown in their relationship.

This is a pretty significant addition because it finally gives us a clearer picture of what happened between the two. Grog wasn't simply a rebellious young man who decided to leave home. He had his own dreams and interests, but his father couldn't accept that his son wanted a different future.

After hearing this, you can head into the Lost Woods and follow the original sequence. Grog is still there, seemingly trapped in the same strange state, and showing him Cojiro produces the same reaction as before. He snaps out of it and asks you to take the Odd Mushroom to the Granny's Potion Shop.

However, Granny also has a few new things to say! She confirms that Grog has been acting foolishly by distancing himself from his family, adding another perspective to the conflict. It's a small exchange, but it helps establish that this isn't just a disagreement between a father and son. So yes, the entire family has been affected by Grog's departure.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake has finally been released, and fans have already discovered several game-breaking glitches.

Unfortunately, things take the same tragic turn when you return to the Lost Woods with the medicine. Grog is gone, and Fado is waiting in his place. This time, however, the encounter is considerably more unsettling. She immediately notices the medicine's smell and desperately asks you to hand it over, offering a tool Grog left behind in exchange. Then, she explains that adults who enter the forest and lose their way, just like Grog apparently did, eventually turn into Stalfos.

But the story doesn't quite end there. You can return to Kakariko Village and talk to the Cucco Lady again, who provides even more information about her brother. She explains that she now takes care of the Cuccos because Grog left home after refusing to become a carpenter. In other words, her own life has also been shaped by the same family conflict that drove him away. And she’s also still hopeful that her brother is okay and will be back someday.

Finally, you can take the tool Grog left behind to the Master Craftsman, who is now waiting near the entrance to Gerudo Valley. He recognizes it as something he had given his son and explains that he had asked Grog to return it personally. Instead, his son apparently chose to send someone else to do the job.

It's a rather dismissive reaction, especially considering everything we've learned about their relationship. Even after Grog has disappeared, his father seems more concerned about the way he returned a tool than the fact that he may never see his son again.

What always fascinated me about Grog's story in the original Ocarina of Time was how much the game managed to communicate without ever explicitly explaining anything. It gave us scattered clues, brief conversations, and seemingly unrelated characters who slowly revealed their connections to one another. The rest was left to the players, who spent years discussing theories about Grog, his family, and what might have happened to him.

The remake takes those little pieces and finally puts them together. We now know exactly why Grog left home, what caused the rift with his father, and how his decision affected the rest of his family. And while the game still leaves some things open to interpretation, his story feels much more complete.

What I particularly love about this addition is that it doesn't try to turn Grog into some incredibly important character or give him an elaborate questline that changes the entire adventure. Instead, it simply gives more attention to a person who was already part of Hyrule, allowing us to understand the struggles that were always hiding behind his grumpy attitude.

And there's something genuinely sad about realizing that the Stalfos we encounter throughout the game might have once been people with their own dreams, families, and reasons for entering the forest. Grog's story makes that possibility feel much more personal. After all, he wasn't some nameless traveler who got lost. He was a young man who wanted to follow his own path, but never managed to find a way back home.

We now know exactly why Grog left home, what caused the rift with his father, and how his decision affected the rest of his family. And while the game still leaves some things open to interpretation, his story feels much more complete.

I also love how this expanded story fits into what makes Ocarina of Time so special! Hyrule isn't just a collection of locations for Link to explore, but a world filled with people whose lives continue beyond the moments when we interact with them. Sometimes, all it takes is a few extra lines of dialogue or a character walking to a different spot at sunset to make that world feel considerably richer.

Of course, I still have one personal theory I'd rather believe. Maybe Grog didn't actually turn into a Stalfos. Maybe he discovered the secret entrance to Termina, found his way to Clock Town, and eventually became the Cucco-loving man we meet in Majora's Mask. After all, if there's anyone who deserves a happy ending surrounded by the animals he loves, it's Grog. And after everything this remake has revealed about his family, I think I'll keep believing that version of the story.

#4235. Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't

A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed. Now, scientists at Yale have taken an important step toward identifying which treatments can actually influence biological aging and which ones show little measurable benefit.

Their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests. Popular over-the-counter supplements examined in the research, however, showed little evidence of producing the same effects.

The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.

From Fighting Cancer to Understanding Aging

When Raghav Sehgal began graduate school at Yale several years ago, he planned to use advanced computer science techniques to investigate cancer. His background in engineering and experience launching a computational biology startup had given him a strong foundation for that work.

However, a question from his Ph.D. adviser at the Yale School of Medicine changed his research direction. Rather than focusing on individual diseases such as cancer or cardiovascular disease, why not investigate the aging process that contributes to their development?

"That put me on a different path," said Sehgal, now an associate research scientist in psychiatry who specializes in computational biology and bioinformatics. "As researchers, we have a long way to go in understanding the aging process and whether the steps we take to manage it really work."

Sehgal now studies the biological mechanisms behind human aging, how scientists can measure those changes, and why getting older increases the likelihood of conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and dementia. His work also explores whether interventions might reverse certain aspects of biological aging, even if eliminating aging itself remains beyond reach.

New DNA Tests Reveal Which Anti-Aging Treatments Work

Sehgal is the lead author of the new study, which was conducted in the laboratory of Albert Higgins-Chen, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine. The research team set out to determine which existing approaches to slowing aging produce changes that can be reliably measured.

Their analysis found encouraging results for certain medications and lifestyle interventions. In contrast, the over-the-counter supplements included in the study generally failed to produce meaningful reductions in biological age.

The project involved the entire Higgins-Chen laboratory, including Daniel Borrus, Jenel F. Armstrong, John Gonzalez, Jessica Kasamoto, and Yaroslav Markov.

"For the first time we've shown that certain therapies have measurable impacts," said Sehgal. "This wasn't previously possible, because we didn't have enough data to say these biomarkers are consistently responsive to these interventions."

Biomarkers provide measurable information about what is happening inside the body. In aging research, they can help estimate a person's biological or functional age, which may differ from their chronological age.

To investigate whether treatments could influence aging, the Yale team relied primarily on blood-based measurements called epigenetic clocks.

These tools analyze chemical patterns attached to DNA, particularly methyl groups (basic chemical structures that act like tags). Previous research has shown that these chemical markers change as people grow older. Some interventions may reverse certain age-associated patterns, and computer algorithms use those changes to estimate a person's biological age.

The researchers brought together findings from 51 clinical studies investigating different anti-aging strategies. These ranged from dietary supplements and medications to lifestyle changes and medical procedures.

Across those studies, the team examined more than 110 DNA methylation biomarkers (including 16 major epigenetic clocks). By comparing measurements taken before and after interventions, they could evaluate which approaches were associated with reductions in biological age.

"What we did was pretty unique," Sehgal said. "We already know that certain things might prolong health span and lifespan. There is data from retrospective analysis as well as from animal models. We took all that knowledge along with the real-world clinical studies to identify which interventions in humans were slowing down aging across the board in these known biomarkers."

Which Anti-Aging Treatments Showed the Best Results?

The researchers divided the interventions into four main groups: prescription drugs, lifestyle modifications, over-the-counter supplements, and medical procedures.

One of the clearest findings involved diet and exercise. Combining regular physical activity with a healthy eating plan consistently reduced epigenetic age. The dietary approaches examined included Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb diets.

The strongest reductions in biological age markers were associated with certain pharmaceutical treatments. These included metformin and semaglutide, prescription medications used to manage metabolic conditions and body weight, as well as anti-TNF therapies that target a protein involved in the body's inflammatory response.

(TNF, or tumor necrosis factor, is an immune-system protein that helps fight inflammation-related injury.)

The findings were less encouraging for over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures. In the studies examined, these approaches did not produce measurable reductions in epigenetic age.

The researchers also discovered that newer biological age clocks performed better than older versions. Another important finding was that people living with diseases generally experienced larger changes in their aging biomarkers than healthy participants.

Could DNA Blood Tests Transform Anti-Aging Research?

According to Sehgal, the next priority is to test these findings in larger, more diverse populations. This would help researchers determine how consistently different treatments influence biological aging across people with different health conditions and backgrounds.

The improved blood tests could also dramatically shorten the time needed to evaluate potential anti-aging therapies.

"If these new biomarkers are eventually validated to predict long-term health, scientists will be able to evaluate anti-aging therapies much faster," he added. "Instead of waiting decades for evidence from clinical trials, we'll be able to see which interventions are effective and in which people in a few years or even months."

That possibility could represent a major advance for aging research. Instead of relying entirely on clinical studies that follow participants for decades, scientists might eventually use validated biological age measurements to identify promising treatments much earlier.

However, senior author Higgins-Chen stressed that scientists must be careful about interpreting what changes in aging biomarkers actually mean.

"We have developed a rigorous, systematic approach to evaluating and comparing how biomarkers change across a wide variety of interventions, and that is a critical step in the right direction," he said. "However, the true meaning of that change must be fully understood."

Important Questions About Slowing Aging Remain

Although the results are promising, several major questions remain unanswered.

For example, researchers still need to establish whether changes in biological age are directly caused by a treatment or influenced by other factors that were not accounted for. They also need to understand how quickly those changes occur, whether they persist after treatment ends, and which biological processes produce them.

Most importantly, scientists have not yet established whether lowering epigenetic age leads to meaningful improvements in long-term health.

"And most importantly - what does the change mean for our long-term risk of age-related disease and functional decline?" Higgins-Chen said.

Further investigations into these questions are underway, with additional studies led by Borrus, Armstrong, and Grace Zou.

The Higgins-Chen laboratory is also affiliated with Yale's Department of Pathology, the Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Program, and the Y-Age Yale Center for Research on Aging.

What Appears to Work Against Biological Aging?

Based on the improved DNA-based blood tests, the Yale researchers identified two particularly promising approaches for reducing biological age markers:

The analysis also identified benefits from certain anti-TNF medications, while the tested over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures showed little measurable effect.

These results provide a clearer picture of which interventions may influence biological aging. However, more research is needed to confirm the findings and determine whether reductions in biological age markers ultimately translate into fewer age-related diseases, better health, or longer lives.

#4234. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

#4233. Broken Ranks beginners guide - Everything you need to know to get started

At first glance, Broken Ranks looks like a classic isometric RPG, but the moment you set foot in the game, nostalgia almost immediately follows. Inspired by the golden age of CRPGs, this MMORPG combines nostalgic visuals with tactical, turn-based combat, a dark fantasy setting, and cross-platform progression.

Like any MMO worth its salt, Broken Ranks gives you plenty  to consider from the first second you start playing: What class will you play? What skills should you use? And most importantly, how to get stronger? These are the questions this guide will answer. And, because Broken Ranks is not as simple as blindly following the quest line, we’ll be shedding some light on the most unique features it has to offer.

Picking Your Class Broken Ranks features seven classes, each with a completely different skill set and value in groups. Of course, if you are a seasoned RPG player, chances are you already know what class you like; however, if you’re a complete beginner, you can find an overview of each class below:

Whichever class you pick, bear in mind that you should choose based on what you like, not what is meta. If you want to be useful to the group (or you play with a friend), then picking a Knight or a Druid is ideal. However, it’s not mandatory. As a solo player, anything can work as long as you have fun with it.

There’s no objectively bad choice here, just different preferences and playstyles. Know the trade-offs upfront, and you’ll spend less time second-guessing and more time playing.

Understanding what makes Broken Ranks different Broken Ranks isn't a game that holds your hand. It rewards players who pay attention, think ahead, and learn from their mistakes. So, don't be disappointed if you die during your second encounter (somehow). The game relies heavily on player skill and tactical decision-making, and that's precisely what makes it so enjoyable.

Combat is turn-based and tactical. Think chess on steroids, with a 10-second round to plan your next move. You need to have a strategy in mind, even when facing enemies you've encountered before. And if something doesn't work, you'll need to adapt quickly.

But combat isn't the only thing that makes Broken Ranks stand out. Its world is just as interesting, drawing inspiration from Slavic mythology and low fantasy. Navigation is straightforward: simply tap where you want to go on mobile or click your destination on PC..

The quests are another highlight. Don't expect to be saving kingdoms every ten minutes. Some of the game's best writing revolves around ordinary people with surprisingly unusual problems, whether that's untangling someone's romantic troubles, rigging a local village election, or searching for a missing drunk in a well.

It’s also worth noting that most of the early game, including quests and exploration can be enjoyed solo and at your own pace. You're not forced into groups, giving you plenty of time to explore the world, understand your character, and experiment with different tactics.

How combat in Broken Ranks works - the part that surprises most people Chess on steroids is the shortest accurate description. Here’s the longer one.

When a fight starts, you have 10 seconds per round to plan your actions. You distribute action points (AP) between your attack skills and three defense zones - melee, ranged, and mental. More AP on an attack increases your chance to hit; more AP on defense lowers the chance of taking that type of damage.

On top of that, you’re managing stamina and mana, depending on your class and the skills you use. If you’re short, the action simply doesn’t happen - wasted AP, wasted round. Both resources regenerate a bit at the end of each round, so there’s a constant rhythm of planning what you can actually afford to do.

Combat gets another layer at level 7, when a quest unlocks Rage - a fourth resource that builds every time luck goes against you (yup, that’s a factor too). If you miss an attack or you take a heavy hit, the bar fills. Once it’s maxed out, you can spend it on one of three Special Skills:  A guaranteed strike that acts before everyone else A recovery that restores your resources mid-fight A reflex boost that lets you avoid incoming damage

It’s the game rewarding you for bad luck (your character gets pissed off, just like you do) - and that alone adds a satisfying rhythm to even the roughest encounters.

Outside combat, you can save preferred skill setups as tactics - preset rotations you can select at the start of a fight and tweak during the 10-second window. This makes farming significantly smoother, but also adapting to tougher fights, rather than starting from scratch every time.

It’s a system built for people who like thinking over reacting. It’s also why the game translates well to mobile. PvP is optional, but addictive You are not forced to PvP in Broken Ranks, but it’s extremely fun if you do. If you opt to stay in peaceful mode, no one can touch you outside designated zones. The faction system is there if you want it; it’s never pushed on you.

If you do decide to PvP, you should have some knowledge about the other classes, because chances are, you will encounter them. You always want to know what the best tactics are for dealing with each, so knowledge about that is clutch.

F2P vs premium - what actually matters Broken Ranks uses Platinum as its premium currency. You can purchase it with real money or obtain it through the in-game economy by trading valuable items with other players on the marketplace.

The good news is that you don't necessarily need to spend money to enjoy the game. Free-to-play players can still progress and participate in the MMORPG experience.

A premium account does, however, offer several convenience bonuses, including additional backpack capacity, faster regeneration, and daily rewards. These can make progression smoother, particularly if you spend a lot of time playing.

Ultimately, premium is worth considering if you want to save time and get more convenience out of your sessions, but it isn't something you should feel pressured to purchase when starting out. A few Broken Ranks tips to know before you start Below you will find some additional tips to help you progress:

Broken Ranks is a game made by a Polish indie studio with obvious love for what they’re building. It doesn’t compete with the giants of the genre on budget or scale - it competes on atmosphere, depth, and a combat system unlike anything else in the mobile MMO space. If that sounds like your kind of thing, there’s never been a better time to find out.
